newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court in Atlanta set to hear Noriega appeal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court in Atlanta set to hear Noriega appeal.

text.p: Attorneys for former Panamanian strongman Manuel Noriega will ask a federal appellate court on Wednesday to throw out the deposed dictator's 1992 conviction on drug-trafficking and racketeering charges.

During oral arguments before the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, defence attorneys also were expected to ask a three-judge panel to grant Noriega a new trial on grounds that his original verdict was tainted by a $1.25 million payment to a federal witness linked to the Cali drug cartel.

Noriega, who was 58 at the time of his seven-month trial, is serving a 40-year prison sentence for his conviction on eight of 10 counts in a drug-smuggling and racketeering indictment returned against him by a federal grand jury in Miami.
After the indictment, former President George Bush ordered his capture during the 1989 U.S. invasion of Panama, dubbed by Pentagon officials as Operation Just Cause.
Unless his conviction were overturned, Noriega would remain in prison until he was at least 83 years old.
"The court was misled by the government," said attorney Jon May, who has been defending Noriega along with defence counsel Frank Rubino.
"General Noriega did not recieve a fair trial. We're hoping to get a reversal of his conviction," May said.

The former Panamanian leader was not due to appear in court for the proceedings, which would entail public arguments in the morning followed by a closed-door hearing later in the day to examine classified U.S. government material.

May said the defence case against the conviction would concentrate on an earlier federal court decision that denied Noriega the chance to present his wealth as payment for services rendered to the U.S. government as a CIA informant during the 1980s.
At the original trial, federal prosecutors said Noriega amassed a fortune of $10 million by effectively turning Panama into a way station for Colombia's Medellin drug cartel.

"Essentially, the court found that the defence had to have records of payments by the U.S. government, which is just ridiculous. There wouldn't be any records of payments for these kinds of activities," said May.

"The government was not required to show records of payments by the Medellin cartel. The government was permitted to show the general was involved in drug-trafficking and then allowed the jury to take this leap that the money he had amassed during the early 1980s came from drug-trafficking."
Federal officials say Noriega received $800,000 as a payed CIA informant.
The defence also was expected to argue for a new trial on grounds that the jury which convicted Noriega never learned of a $1.25 million payoff to a federal witness who testified against him.
Noriega's attorneys say the witness was provided by the Cali drug cartel, a Medellin rival.

"The United States government entered into a secret agreement with the Cali cartel to obtain a dynamite witness against General Noriega. They bribed a witness. They paid $1.25 million to get the testimony," said May.

"This was all hidden from the defence. We feel very confident that had the jury known about this deal-with-the- devil between the United States and the Cali cartel, and if they had known about the bribe paid to a government witness, that the verdict would have been very different."
An earlier defence motion for a new trial, based on the same claim, was denied by federal court after a March hearing.
